planting.note: Plant a container-grown grafted tree in spring after all danger of frost, in full sun and well-drained soil away from low-lying frost pockets.

directions: Waldin is one of the oldest named Florida dooryard avocados still commonly planted, valued for its early-to-midseason harvest and reliable heavy bearing on a vigorous, wind-tolerant tree. Fruit is medium to large, smooth-skinned, and pear-shaped with pale green, watery-textured flesh typical of the West Indian race, which lends good tolerance of Florida's hot, humid lowland conditions but less cold tolerance than Mexican-race cultivars. As a Type A flowering cultivar it benefits from a nearby Type B pollinator for heavier fruit set. Choose Waldin where summer heat and salt-air exposure near the coast are bigger concerns than winter cold, since it lacks the frost hardiness of Mexican-race selections.

planting.note: Plant divisions or pups after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from wind.

directions: FHIA-03 is a tetraploid hybrid banana bred by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf spot and Panama disease, the pathogens that most limit backyard banana growing in the humid Gulf South. Unlike its sibling Goldfinger (FHIA-01), FHIA-03 produces a starchier, dual-purpose fruit that can be eaten cooked when green or sweet when fully ripe, giving gardeners flexibility similar to a plantain. The plant regrows readily from the rhizome after a freeze knocks back the pseudostem, making it a practical choice where winter dieback is expected most years. Give it heavy summer feeding and constant soil moisture to reach fruiting size within a single warm season.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown shrub in spring in full sun to light shade, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil.

directions: Pineapple Gem is one of the few genuinely self-fertile feijoa selections, so a single plant can set a worthwhile crop without a second cultivar nearby, unlike most feijoas that need cross-pollination for heavy fruiting. The compact, rounded shrub carries silvery evergreen foliage year-round and edible, sweet spring flowers before setting small, intensely aromatic fruit in fall. It suits gardeners with limited space who still want reliable feijoa production, or a large container that can be moved to shelter in the coldest zone 8 winters. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit with only minor twig damage.

planting.note: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in spring after frost danger, in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil.

directions: Redlands Tropic Star was released by University of Florida breeders working near the Redland agricultural district south of Miami and combines the fragrant, deep-purple fruit of common passion fruit with improved tolerance of the fungal diseases that plague vines in Florida's humid growing season. It is a vigorous, self-fertile climber that needs a strong trellis or arbor, since a single plant can cover a large structure within its first year. Fruit ripens over a long summer-to-fall season and drops when fully ripe, signaling harvest time without guesswork. Choose this cultivar over unnamed seedling passion fruit when disease pressure has been a recurring problem in the garden.
sources: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services

planting.note: Transplant seedlings in spring once soil and air are reliably warm, in full sun and well-drained soil in a frost-free spot.

directions: Waimanalo was developed by the University of Hawaii as a low-branching, compact papaya bred to resist mechanical damage and reduce losses from fruit fly infestation compared to older Hawaiian selections. The medium-large, round-to-oval fruit has thick orange flesh with good sugar content, and the short, sturdy trunk starts fruiting closer to the ground than many other papaya types, easing harvest. It performs best in a warm, sheltered spot with fast-draining soil, since papayas are highly susceptible to root rot in wet ground. Gulf Coast growers usually treat it as a fast-fruiting annual or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
